title: The board slide that says 400%
scenario:
You are an operations lead at a logistics company. For three months you piloted an AI tool that reads supplier documents and fills in order data. Before the pilot, the team agreed on a success target: at least 95% of documents read correctly, on the real mix of documents.

A colleague drafted the board slide. You must fix it before it goes up. The exhibit shows the slide and the data behind it.
exhibit:
DRAFT BOARD SLIDE (made-up example data)
  "AI document reading: 98% accurate, 70% faster, ROI 400%"

DATA BEHIND THE SLIDE
  Main test: 100 supplier documents, all clean typed PDFs.
    Read correctly: 98.
  Real mix last quarter: 65% clean PDFs, 35% scans and photos.
  Small test on scans: 20 scans, 14 read correctly (70%).
  Target set before the pilot: 95% correct on the real mix.

YEARLY FIGURES
  Time saved, counted as the vendor does: $50,000
  Licence and usage: $10,000
  Extra staff review of scans: $14,000 (not on the slide)
  A misread order costs about $120 to correct after delivery.
  Slide ROI: (50,000 - 10,000) / 10,000 = 400%

questions.prompt: What is wrong with the headline "98% accurate"?

options.text: It is fine, because 98 of 100 test documents were read correctly.
options.explanation: The count is right, but the test used only the easiest documents.

options.text: The test used only clean files; with 35% scans at 70%, real accuracy is near 88%.
options.explanation: Right. 0.65 × 98% + 0.35 × 70% is about 88%, below the 95% target. This is our arithmetic. The OpenAI docs list test data that does not match production traffic as an anti-pattern.

options.text: It is too low, because the tool will keep getting better over time.
options.explanation: Future gains are not evidence. A report shows what was measured.

options.text: It is wrong only because 100 test files are too few to measure anything.
options.explanation: A small test is a limit, but the bigger problem is that the mix does not match real work.

questions.prompt: Using the exhibit's yearly figures, what is the ROI once review time is counted as a cost?

options.explanation: This takes (50,000 - 14,000 - 10,000) and divides by the licence alone. The review cost belongs in the total cost too.
This takes the review cost off the benefit, but leaves the $10,000 licence out of the net.
This is the slide's figure. It leaves out the $14,000 review cost.
Right. Net benefit is 50,000 - 24,000 = 26,000, and 26,000 ÷ 24,000 is about 108%. The $50,000 itself is the vendor's way of counting, so the true figure may be lower.

questions.prompt: How should the 20-scan result be shown on the slide?

options.text: Show "70% (14 of 20 scans)" and say a bigger scan test is needed.
options.explanation: Right. The sample size is shown, and the limit is stated. Anthropic's post says not to take scores at face value.

options.text: Leave it out, because 20 files are too few to say anything.
options.explanation: This hides the weakest result on the group that makes up 35% of real work.

options.text: Present it as proof that the AI can never read scans.
options.explanation: 20 files are a hint, not proof. A larger test could change the number.

options.text: Replace it with the vendor's accuracy figure for scans.
options.explanation: A vendor figure is a claim. It was not measured on your documents.

questions.prompt: Which recommendation fits the evidence and OpenAI's accuracy guide best?

options.text: Approve a full rollout now, since 98% beats the 95% target on the test.
options.explanation: The 98% came from clean files only. The target is for the real mix.

options.text: Reject the tool altogether, because 70% on scans counts as a failure.
options.explanation: This ignores the strong clean-document result. It is all or nothing.

options.text: Approve clean documents only; keep scans with staff and re-test them.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's guide shows a human staying in charge where failure is costly. Here the scans stay with people until they pass the test.

options.text: Approve a full rollout and review the scans after the first year.
options.explanation: A wrong read costs money now. Waiting a year to look at the weak group is too late.
